title: Possible gap in Proposition 5.10 (Torsor Cartier strictness)
body: **Summary:** The certificate and framework check out, but Proposition 5.10 appears to fail on the weight-0 functions the slope inequality measures: Frobenius also acts on the weight factor, so full-order ℓ-poles show up outside the claimed prime windows. The same test on the raw rows passes, which points to the decomposition in (51). Details and scripts below. Hi Christopher, I spent some time with the hybrid arithmetic holonomy paper and wanted to share something I ran into, in case it's useful. I'm genuinely more interested in unsolved problems than settled ones, which is exactly why this paper caught my attention. First, what checks out: I recomputed the margin independently from the displayed formulas and reproduced your certificate exactly (0.1317993568… at p = 5, s = 5). Plugging CDT's published cost into your framework also recovers exactly the known results (ζ₂(3), ζ₂(5), ζ₃(3)) and gives a small positive margin for ζ₅(3), which is a nice consistency check on the setup. Where I got stuck is Proposition 5.10. The Dwork relation in Lemma 3.4 holds for the raw rows R_e, and I confirmed it numerically. For the weight-0 functions whose jets enter the slope inequality (for example CDT's H = E*·K and its derivatives in the Hauptmodul), it seems to fail, because Frobenius also acts on the weight factor: at ℓ = 17, s = 5, H(q) − ℓ⁻⁵H(q^ℓ) has ℓ⁻⁵ poles from q¹⁷ on. Testing the window conclusion of 5.10 directly on that space, I find pivots with full-order ℓ-poles far from any multiple of ℓ (for example s = 9, ℓ = 37, n = 55). As a control, the same code on your raw rows finds none, so the Taylor / no-backflow lemmas look fine; the issue seems to be the decomposition in (51). Since C in Proposition 5.10 is a fixed constant, a single D can't rule out a larger one, so I also measured, for each D, the smallest C that would put every ℓ-pole pivot inside its window (ℓ > 1.2D, which covers all your certified ξ): | s | D = 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 | 18 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 5 | 6 | 11 | 15 | 19 | 22 | | 9 | 15 | 22 | | | | The C needed grows linearly with D, and p = 3 gives the same numbers. The raw-row control needs C = 0 at every D (6, 12, 18). This was computed with independent code (exact arithmetic mod ℓ^K, a different η), which also reproduces my first pivot test exactly. Here is the mechanism drawn in Lean Studio. Each square is a coefficient qⁿ, and red means ℓ divides its denominator. The Dwork step cancels the poles of the raw row J, which sit on multiples of ℓ. In H = E*·K the weight factor E* moves them onto q^{ℓ+1}, q^{ℓ+2}, …, where ℓ⁻ˢH(q^ℓ) has nothing to cancel them. The blue bands mark where Proposition 5.10 allows a pivot to carry an ℓ-pole. The root cause is checked by Lean's kernel (core Lean, no Mathlib): for p = 2, s = 5, ℓ = 17, J(q) − 17⁻⁵J(q¹⁷) is 17-integral through q⁶⁰, while every coefficient from q¹⁷ to q⁶⁰ of H(q) − 17⁻⁵H(q¹⁷) has v₁₇ = −5. The reason is one line: J₁₇ = 1 + 17⁻⁵ and E*₄ = … + 1·q + …, so the product puts the pole on q¹⁸. The scripts are short, standard-library Python plus mpmath, and I'm happy to share them, and the small Lean project, or walk through them. If they'd be useful, I can also open a PR adding them under scripts/ so you can run them yourself. It's quite possible I'm misreading how the torsor chart is meant to work, in which case I'd like to understand it. This analysis was done with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic) and Lean Studio. Keith
